paragraphs.heading: A storm built around low pressure
paragraphs.text: A tropical cyclone is a fast-spinning storm system built around an area of low pressure, with strong winds and thunderstorms set in a spiral that bring heavy rain and squalls. It has a warm core and forms over tropical or subtropical seas without being tied to a weather front. A well-defined centre is ringed by deep convection, with winds circling it in a closed loop at the surface. Forecasters say one has formed once average surface winds pass 35 kn (65 km/h; 40 mph).

paragraphs.heading: One storm, many names
paragraphs.text: The same kind of storm goes by different names depending on where it is and how strong it is. A strong one is a hurricane in the Atlantic or northeastern Pacific and a typhoon in the northwestern Pacific, while in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific it is simply a tropical cyclone. It may also be called a tropical storm, a cyclonic storm or a tropical depression, and Indian Ocean storms can be called severe cyclonic storms.

paragraphs.heading: Running on warm water
paragraphs.text: These storms usually form over large areas of fairly warm water and take their energy from it. Water evaporates from the sea surface, and when the moist air rises and cools it condenses into cloud and rain. That sets them apart from mid-latitude storms such as nor'easters, which are driven mostly by horizontal differences in temperature. To grow, the young thunderstorms need sea temperatures of around 27 °C (81 °F), little vertical wind shear, unstable and humid air, and enough Coriolis force to build a low-pressure centre.

paragraphs.heading: Where the spin comes from
paragraphs.text: As air flows inward toward the centre, it keeps the angular momentum it picked up from Earth's rotation, and that drives the strong rotating winds. That is why cyclones rarely form within 5° of the equator. The winds whirl around a clear central eye, clockwise south of the equator and counterclockwise north of it, a difference caused by the Coriolis effect.

paragraphs.heading: How one is born
paragraphs.text: Most begin in the Intertropical Convergence Zone, a broad low-pressure area where winds blow from the northeast or southeast. Air warmed over the ocean rises in separate pockets, building tall thunderstorms. These usually fade fast, but they can gather into big clusters, setting up a flow of warm, moist, rising air that starts to turn as it interacts with Earth's rotation. Each year about 86 reach tropical storm strength worldwide; 47 pass 119 km/h (74 mph), and 20 become intense storms of at least Category 3 on the Saffir–Simpson scale.

paragraphs.heading: Wind, water and a warming world
paragraphs.text: Coasts take the worst of it, from high waves, storm surges, tornadoes, and strong winds and rain, while inland areas suffer far less damage, though flooding is felt everywhere. A cyclone pulls in air from a wide area and wrings its water out as rain over a much smaller one. As fresh moist air keeps arriving, extremely heavy rain can last for hours or days up to 40 km (25 mi) from the coast, flooding rivers and swamping local water control systems. Scientists have found that climate change, by warming the oceans and intensifying the water cycle, can make these storms last longer, happen more often and grow stronger.
